name: Lenten fasting

card.summary: The Christian pre-Easter fasting season, in which reduced or plant-based eating and calorie restriction over about 40 days can change body weight and metabolic markers.
card.note: Strict versions exclude all animal products, so protein and nutrient planning matters, especially for lifters and people with diabetes.

quick.overview:
Lent is a roughly 40-day season of prayer, almsgiving and fasting before Easter. Its fasting rules vary by tradition, from limiting meat on certain days in Western churches to a vegan-style diet in Eastern and Oriental Orthodox practice.

For appearance, it matters because the eating pattern can lower weight and body mass index and shift blood markers over several weeks. Small studies of Ethiopian and Egyptian Christians have measured exactly these changes, and lifters on forums discuss how to keep muscle while observing it.
quick.how: Practice depends on denomination. Catholics abstain from meat on Ash Wednesday and Fridays, with fasting on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday. Orthodox believers commonly avoid meat, fish, eggs and dairy for the season, and Coptic practice can include fasting until sunset. Lifters who observe the fast describe leaning on nuts, legumes and shellfish where permitted to get protein.
quick.risks: Strict plant-based fasting can make protein intake hard to maintain, a concern raised by trainees on forums. Clinicians studying fasting Christians with type 2 diabetes have measured its effect on glucose control. Exemptions exist for the young, old, pregnant and ill in the churches' own rules.

lead: Lenten fasting is the fasting and abstinence observed by Christians during Lent, a 40-day season of penitence before Easter modelled on Jesus's fast in the desert. It is built around prayer, fasting and almsgiving.[5]

Although its purpose is religious, the diet pattern it produces draws interest from people who care about body composition. Studies of Orthodox fasters have measured weight, body mass index and biochemical markers before and after the fast.[1][2] Strength-training forum members who observe it discuss maintaining training and protein during the season.[6][7]

angle.text: People do not generally enter Lent for looks, but the shift to a largely plant-based diet is associated in studies with weight loss and metabolic changes. Lifters discuss how to keep muscle on while observing it.

paras: Lent is counted differently by tradition. The Roman Rite begins on Ash Wednesday and, since 1970, counts 44 days through Holy Thursday; Eastern Orthodox Great Lent runs 40 days from Clean Monday; Coptic practice has eight weeks of fasting in three parts.[5]

Catholics since 1966 are bound to fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday and abstain from meat on Fridays, with further fasting encouraged; before 1966 the rules were stricter. Orthodox fasting avoids meat, fish, eggs and dairy and is therefore vegetarian or vegan, and Coptic practice traditionally includes abstaining from food and drink until sunset.[5]

Early Christian writings describe pre-Easter fasting. Athanasius described a 40-day fast across the church in 339 AD, and the Council of Laodicea around 363-364 described Lenten fasting as a necessity. Scholars differ on whether the 40-day form dates from Nicaea in 325.[5]

On T Nation, an Orthodox lifter explains that he fasts for religious reasons and describes asceticism as the purpose.[6] Other threads ask about training on low protein during the fast and note that strict observance without meat, fish, dairy and eggs makes protein hard to find, with nuts and shellfish suggested by other posters.[8] Posts also discuss Catholic Friday abstinence rules and their history.[4][7]

A study of Ethiopian Orthodox Christians following a short-term vegan Lenten diet examined weight, body mass index and biochemical parameters by gender and time.[1] A prospective study in Egypt assessed the effect of the Lenten fast on anthropometric, biochemical and glycaemic measures in Christians with type 2 diabetes.[2] A further cohort study of Ethiopian Orthodox fasting looked at appetite hormones, insulin sensitivity and beta-cell function in healthy people and people with diabetes.[3]

timeline.event: Athanasius describes a 40-day fast observed across the church.[5]
Council of Laodicea calls Lenten fasting a requirement.[5]
Catholic obligatory fasting reduced to Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, with Friday meat abstinence.[5]
Code of Canon Law sets fasting for ages 18-59 and abstinence from age 14.[5]

lore.intro: Lifters on T Nation discuss Lent mainly as a logistics question of protein and training during a religious fast.[6][8]

claims.claim: Fasting disciplines the body and mind
claims.believers: An Orthodox poster says fasting follows Christ's teaching and brings the body to discipline so the soul can engage.[6]
claims.experts: This is a religious claim outside the scope of the clinical literature, which measures weight and metabolic markers.[1][2]

claims.claim: Strict Lent makes it hard to get enough protein for training
claims.believers: Forum members note that removing meat, fish, dairy and eggs leaves nuts and shellfish as main options.[8]
claims.experts: Studies of Lenten vegan diets report changes in weight and biochemical parameters during the fast.[1]
